decisions.question: e-11675

source.question: e-11675
source.value:
We wish to find the limits of integration $u_1(x,y)$ and $u_2(x,y)$ such that

$$
\int_0^1 \int_0^{2} \int_0^{\sqrt[3]{z}}  f(x,y,z) \:\textrm{d}y\:\textrm{d}x\:\textrm{d}z
=
\iint\limits_D \left[ \int_{u_1(x,y)}^{u_2(x,y)} f(x,y,z) \:\textrm{d}z\right] \textrm{d}A.
$$

From the repeated integral, we see that the region of integration $R$ can be written as a type III region as follows:

$$
R = \big\{
(x,y,z) \:\: {:} \:\: 0 \leq x \leq 2, \:\: 0 \leq z \leq 1, \:\: 0 \leq y \leq \sqrt[3]{z} 
\big\}
$$

To change the order of integration from $\textrm{d}y\:\textrm{d}x\:\textrm{d}z$ to $\textrm{d}z\:\textrm{d}A,$ we write $R$ as a type I region.

To visualize this, imagine firing an arrow through the region parallel to the $z$-axis and in the direction of increasing $z,$ as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14073682/assets/efc1013a8202f8eea26250b904cf3d4672b30d478ddaad72b6347b274bd33f7d.png)

The arrow enters the region through the bottom boundary and leaves through the top boundary:

- The bottom boundary of the region, written in the form $z=z(x,y),$ is

$$
y = \sqrt[3]{z}, \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
z = y^3.
$$

- The top boundary of the region is $z = 1.$

Therefore, the type I representation of $R$ is

$$
R = \big\{
(x,y,z) \:\: {:} \:\: (x,y) \in D, \:\: y^3\leq z \leq 1
\big\},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14073682/assets/3ae61409e70d4d6d6227a306ab1651331d9b40633248fd525cefbab519202a52.png)

Therefore, by swapping the order of integration so that it is integrated first with respect to $z$ and then over $D,$ we obtain

$$
\int_0^1 \int_0^{2} \int_0^{\sqrt[3]{z}} f(x,y,z) \:\textrm{d}y\:\textrm{d}x\:\textrm{d}z
=
\iint\limits_D \left[\int_{y^3}^{1} f(x,y,z) \:\textrm{d}z\right] \textrm{d}A.
$$

decisions.question: e-11676

source.question: e-11676
source.value:
We wish to find limits of integration $u_1(x,y),$ $u_2(x,y),$ $v_1(x),$ $v_2(x),$ $a,$ and $b$ such that

$$
\int_0^{1} \int_0^{1} \int_0^{1-z^2} f(x,y,z) \:\textrm{d}y\:\textrm{d}z\:\textrm{d}x
=
\int_a^b \int_{v_1(x)}^{v_2(x)} \int_{u_1(x,y)}^{u_2(x,y)} f(x,y,z) \:\textrm{d}z\:\textrm{d}y\:\textrm{d}x.
$$

From the repeated integral, we see that the region of integration $R$ can be written as a type III region as follows:

$$
R = \left\{ (x,y,z) \: : \: 0 \leq x \leq 1, \:\: 0 \leq z \leq 1, \:\: 0 \leq y \leq 1-z^2 \right\}
$$

Now, let's sketch the region. Since it is a type III region, we first draw the projection onto the $xz$-plane, given by

$$
E = \left\{
(x,z) \: : \: 0 \leq x \leq 1, \:\: 0 \leq z \leq 1
\right\}
$$

as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14073682/assets/8007b0f7348f9855a009aff56c676122a739e6210d4f024c524e72e3cfa23312.png)

Then, the region $R$ is shown in the diagram below, where $0 \leq y \leq  1-z^2.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14073682/assets/97d0f5fc56498e1a044dbbfc07da571c1806903822dfdb1d68f877723ce9a559.png)

To change the order of integration from $\textrm{d}y\:\textrm{d}z\:\textrm{d}x$ to $\textrm{d}z\:\textrm{d}y\:\textrm{d}x,$ we write $R$ as a type I region and its projection $D$ onto the $xy$-plane as a type I *plane* region.

To visualize this, imagine firing an arrow through the region parallel to the $z$-axis and in the direction of increasing $z,$ as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14073682/assets/f5fab194951b50a2a0c81aff8d422b98be5145bbef3123ea746b86bcebd1e778.png)

The arrow enters the region through the bottom boundary and leaves through the top boundary:

- The top boundary of the region, written in the form $z=z(x,y),$ is

$$
y = 1-z^2
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
z = \sqrt{1- y}.
$$

- The bottom boundary of the region is $z=0.$

Therefore, the type I representation of $R$ is

$$
R = \big\{ (x,y,z) \: : \: (x,y) \in D, \:\: 0 \leq z \leq \sqrt{1-y} \big\},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14073682/assets/403675d42fae7e437e62bcb3e254e3f7cf3997556606ed529807d83253d1c439.png)

Now, we consider the projection $D$ as a type I plane region in the $xy$-plane with the top curve given by $y=1.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14073682/assets/1e1fbae22c5ad39225a5de4e3c3aeb025cb41b21bbf0c127da57e3ada10c3087.png)

Hence, we have that

$$
D = \left\{ (x,y) \: : \: 0 \leq x \leq 1, \:\: 0 \leq y \leq 1 \right\}.
$$

Therefore, by swapping the order of integration so that it is integrated first with respect to $z,$ then $y,$ then $x,$ we obtain

$$
\int_0^{1} \int_0^{1} \int_0^{1-z^2} f(x,y,z) \:\textrm{d}y\:\textrm{d}z\:\textrm{d}x
=
\int_0^{1} \int_0^{\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{1}} \int_{\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{0}}^{\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\sqrt{1-y}}} f(x,y,z) \:\textrm{d}z\:\textrm{d}y\:\textrm{d}x.
$$

decisions.question: e-12405

source.question: e-12405
source.value:
We cannot integrate the given integral because we cannot find a simple antiderivative of the integrand. So, we change the order of integration.

We wish to find the limits of integration $u_1(x,y),$ $u_2(x,y),$ $v_1(y),$ $v_2(y),$ $a,$ and $b$ such that

$$
\int_{0}^{1} \int_{0}^{2} \int_{z}^{2} e^{x^2} \, \mathrm{d}x \: \mathrm{d}z \: \mathrm{d}y
=
\int_{a}^{b} \int_{v_1(y)}^{v_2(y)} \int_{u_1(x,y)}^{u_2(x,y)} e^{x^2} \, \textrm{d}z \: \textrm{d}x \: \textrm{d}y.
$$

From the repeated integral, we see that the region of integration $R$ can be written as a type II region as follows:

$$
R = \left\{ (x,y,z) \: : \: 0 \leq y \leq 1, \:\: 0 \leq z \leq 2, \:\: z \leq x \leq 2 \right\}
$$

Now, let's sketch the region. Since it is a type II region, we first sketch the projection onto the $yz$-plane, given by

$$
E = \left\{ (y,z) \: : \: 0 \leq y \leq 1, \:\: 0 \leq z \leq 2 \right\}
$$

as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14073682/assets/9fe61cd50d31086b47495f0bd0fd71308fc30286d392f4d0064cf743b93272b0.png)

Then, the region $R$ is shown in the diagram below, where $z \leq x \leq 2.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14073682/assets/6af345af2d33b53c698e8e1d4eff10e3b3116911e14ee1b4581da7eee8528f94.png)

To change the order of integration from $\mathrm{d}x \: \mathrm{d}z \: \mathrm{d}y$ to $\textrm{d}z\:\textrm{d}x\:\textrm{d}y,$ we write $R$ as a type I region and its projection $D$ onto the $xy$-plane as a type II *plane* region.

To visualize this, imagine firing an arrow through the region parallel to the $z$-axis and in the direction of increasing $z,$ as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14073682/assets/53ec4e56ca38362b10c05d4cc657f9057005d9692e0fcde1f0846e7e80b4f478.png)

The arrow enters the region through the bottom boundary and leaves through the top boundary:

- The bottom boundary of the region is

$$
z=0.
$$

- The top boundary of the region, written in the form $z = z(x,y),$ is

$$
x = z \qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad z = x.
$$

Therefore, the type I representation of $R$ is

$$
R = \left\{ (x,y,z) \: : \: (x,y) \in D, \:\: 0 \leq z \leq x \right\},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14073682/assets/5ce67f398f60237d763d393d62f9e7346270b954acc7efdc7a096a5f3155f4d3.png)

Now, we consider the projection $D$ as a type II plane region in the $xy$-plane with the left curve given by $x = 0.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14073682/assets/0dbf7a35fe74730db7c2a07fc4bbe881a66412cee53bf0a606c522f5493e58c2.png)

Hence,

$$
D = \left\{ (x,y) \: : \: 0 \leq x \leq 2, \:\: 0 \leq y \leq 1 \right\}.
$$

Therefore, by swapping the order of integration, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{z}^{2}{e}^{{x}^{2}}\,dx\,dz\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{x}{e}^{{x}^{2}}\,dz\,dx\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}{e}^{{x}^{2}}[{\int }_{0}^{x}\text{d}z]\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}{e}^{{x}^{2}}[z]_{0}^{x}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}x{e}^{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{2}x{e}^{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[\frac{1}{2}{e}^{{x}^{2}}]}_{0}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}({e}^{4}-1)\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{2}({e}^{4}-1)\cdot [y]_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}({e}^{4}-1).\end{aligned}
$$
